Precious Metals Quarterly 2010 Q2 

# Executive summary 

## Gold: prices to stay above $1,000/oz 

The gold market’s fundamental surplus reached 1,554t in 2009 – more than double the 678t seen in 2008 – as supply continued to run ahead of fabrication demand.  The surplus is expected to remain large throughout the forecast period with a modest reduction expected in 2010 (due to a correction in the unusually large changes in both scrap supply and jewellery demand in 2009 Q1), before increasing again in 2011-13 and tailing off just a little in 2014. 

After a second year of growth, total gold supply should continue to increase, although at a slower rate than the 11.3% in 2009, until 2014 when a marginal contraction is expected.  Mine output is expected to have the strongest bearing on the total gold supply, which should increase by an average of about 100 t/y over the forecast period, mainly due to a raft of new mines and expnasion projects which are expected to come on stream during the forecast period offsetting declines in prodution caused by lower grades and disruptions at older existing mines.  In addition, total gold supply will be lifted by smaller contributions from scrap collection and the de-hedging of producers.  However, the official sector expected to move from being a net supplier in 2010 to being a modest net buyer of gold in subsequent forecast years. 

On the demand side, we expect gold offtake from fabricators in 2010 to rebound from the very low levels of 2009, driven by improved demand from the jewellery and electronics sectors. Some reversal is expected during 2011 and 2012 as jewellery demand comes under renewed pressure from the high levels of the gold price.  Jewellery demand is forecast to improve again by 2013, but the impact on broader fabrication demand will be partly offset by reduced demand for coins and medallions as an economic recovery reduces gold’s appeal as a safe haven. Nevertheless, by 2014, the share of coins and medallions in total fabrication demand is expected to be higher than it was in 2006, which will come at the expense of the jewellery sector. 

The gold price is expected to continue rising until it peaks in 2011, before abating in the subsequent forecast years, averaging just under $1,200/oz over the period.  During the past 18 months of financial uncertainty, gold has rallied under the influence of investor inflows, which have not reversed during times of improved market confidence.  Over the next 12-18 months we expect that uncertainty in the financial markets is likely to continue and overshadow periods of economic confidence, resulting in risk aversion demand for gold and providing upside potential to the gold price.  However, we expect the gold price to start drifting lower by late 2011/early 2012 as the economic climate stabilises and the risk appetite of investors returns, resulting in less safe haven buying of gold.

## Other precious metal markets 

### Silver 

No evidence has surfaced during the last three months that leads us to believe that stocks did not swell in 2009.  At almost 5,700 tonnes, the implied level of investor purchases is in fact greater than we previously thought.  And, with this in turn maintaining silver's high price, miners are continuing push forward with plans that will keep supply significantly in excess of fabrication demand. 



- Revisions to government numbers have now made the official figure for Mexican mine production in 2009 consistent with our own.  We are therefore more confident in our belief that most miners’ production plans are coming to pass. 



- Fabrication demand is continuing to recover alongside the recovery in industrial activity. However, having come in more strongly than we being initially feared in the early part of the recovery, the prospect of the economic outlook being downgraded has lifted. 



- This said, any increasing uncertainty regarding the economy could of course sustain investor interest in silver for longer. 

### Platinum 

Platinum’s 18-month up-trend broke in May when prices moved significantly lower.  Fears that economic tightening would hit fabrication demand had more effect than further safe-haven investment.  And we too believe that industrial offtake will be less than we previously thought to 2014.  So prices will have to be generally lower to encourage jewellery to take up this slack. 



- Alongside lower car production and stock reductions right along the manufacturing chain, autocatalyst demand suffered last year from a significant switch from platinum to palladium. 

- Cyclical pressures will reverse at some point, but perhaps not as soon as we thought before. 



- Jewellery will have to grow to 2.4-2.5 Moz/y once net investment tails away. 

### Palladium 

Despite large inflows into ETFs at the start of 2010, palladium prices fell by 25% in the four weeks from early May.  Surpluses remain as endemic as ever and may not reverse until 2014. 



- The same factors which undermined platinum use in autocatalysts last year meant palladium demand held up relatively well. 

- Supply was nonetheless again higher still even before net Russian sales. 



- Although new ETFs have encouraged investment of late, this will struggle to match the surpluses that we forecast in 2011-12.

## Data sources and study team 

The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), GTIS trade statistics, and company websites and written reports. 

However, CRU’s interpretation of these data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources. 

The forecast is exclusively CRU’s.
